opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the way to think about it is to compare against the counterfactual, not against zero. People see a bill for tokens or compute and think, "wow, that's a lot of money for code." But what's the alternative? It's an engineer's time, and engineers are expensive and scarce. Even more than that, it's calendar time. If something that would have taken a team two weeks gets done in an afternoon, the question isn't really whether the API cost was a few hundred dollars. It's what you could do with those two weeks.

So my rough heuristic is to look at throughput and quality together. Are we shipping more things that matter, and are they at least as good as before? If the model writes a bunch of code that someone then has to spend days untangling, that's not a win, even if it looked cheap. But if it lets one person own something that used to need three, or lets a researcher try ten ideas instead of two, that's huge leverage. Usually the cost is a rounding error next to the value of that.

There's also a second-order effect people underrate. When the cost of trying something drops, you try things you never would have bothered with: a quick internal tool, a prototype to settle an argument, a test suite nobody had time to write. Those don't show up neatly in a spreadsheet, but they compound.

The places I'd be more careful are where verification is hard. If you can't easily check whether the output is right, the cheapness of generating it can be misleading, and you have to invest in tests, review, and good evals so you're not just producing plausible-looking code faster. But for most of the work we see, the math isn't close. The bottleneck is people's attention and judgment, and anything that frees those up is worth paying for.

r001.rationale: The response says to compare AI costs against the counterfactual of an engineer’s time, noting that engineers are expensive and scarce.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the way I think about it has shifted a lot over the past couple of years. Early on, the question was framed as "is the model's output worth the tokens?" and you'd do this very literal accounting: here's what we spent on inference, here's how many lines of code came out, does it net out. And that framing turns out to be almost completely wrong, because it treats the engineer's time as free and the tokens as the scarce thing. In reality it's the opposite. A senior engineer at a company like ours costs, fully loaded, several hundred dollars an hour. If spending twenty dollars of compute saves them even fifteen minutes, you've already won.

So the metric I actually care about is something like: what's the throughput of the team on things that matter, and how long does it take an idea to go from someone's head to running in production? And then separately, what does the error rate look like? Because you can move fast and generate a lot of code, but if you're accumulating tech debt or shipping bugs, you're borrowing against the future, and that bill comes due.

The thing that's been striking internally is that the people who get the most out of it aren't the ones who use it to write more code. They're the ones who use it to do things they otherwise wouldn't have done at all. Migrations nobody wanted to touch. Writing the tests for the gnarly module everyone was scared of. Prototyping three approaches in an afternoon instead of arguing about them in a design doc for two weeks. That stuff doesn't show up if you're just measuring tokens-in, lines-out. It shows up as the team being willing to take on harder problems.

Where I'd push back on my own optimism is the review bottleneck. If the model generates a thousand lines and a human has to carefully read all thousand, you haven't saved as much as you think, and you may have actually degraded quality because people skim. So a big part of judging the cost is asking whether you're building the surrounding infrastructure, the tests, the CI, the verification, so that you can actually trust the output without reading every line. If you're not doing that, the real cost isn't the compute, it's the attention you're quietly spending downstream.

r001.rationale: It compares compute spending with the value of human engineering time, stating that $20 of compute can be worthwhile if it saves a senior engineer 15 minutes at several hundred dollars per hour.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at the cost of getting to a working, reliable result, rather than the cost of an individual model call. If you save an engineer a few hours, that can justify quite a lot of inference spending. But if the generated code takes just as long to review and debug as it would have taken to write, then you haven’t really saved anything.

So I’d ask: Are we shipping useful software faster? Are we maintaining quality? And how much human attention does it take to get there? The exciting part is when it makes something worth building that previously would have been too expensive to attempt.

r001.rationale: It compares inference spending with the engineer hours saved and asks whether generated code takes as long to review and debug as writing it, framing cost against the human effort for the same work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to look at it is: what does it cost to get a useful piece of work done? The price of the tokens is one part of that, but so is the engineer’s time reviewing the code, fixing mistakes, and making sure it actually solves the problem.

If you spend more on inference but save hours of engineering time, that can be a very good trade. If you generate a lot of code that takes longer to understand and maintain, it may not be. So I’d measure the whole loop, from the task to something that works, rather than how much code the model produces.

r001.rationale: It weighs token spending against engineering time spent reviewing and fixing the work, and says higher inference costs can be worthwhile when they save engineering hours.
